name: Allocation
problem: How does a program obtain storage for a value, and who is responsible for its initialization and eventual release?

origin.summary: Implementation lineage: language operation, allocator or runtime, storage for a value. Historical invention and priority remain unverified.

mechanism: Allocation obtains storage for values. C exposes byte allocation through malloc; C++ new-expressions also create objects; Rust Box provides owned heap storage; Go delegates storage placement to its implementation. Initialization and release are separate questions whose answers differ between these interfaces.
solutionFamily: Explicit allocation, owned heap storage and implementation-managed storage
costs: Allocation consumes finite storage; C malloc can report failure with a null pointer.
A C allocation needs a matching release; Go's standard runtime performs garbage collection with CPU and memory costs.
transferRule: Compare storage acquisition, initialization, lifetime and release separately. Similar syntax does not imply the same storage placement or failure contract.
confidence: PARTIAL: four language cells directly checked on 2026-09-06 against paired official sources. Historical attribution and the remaining language cells are unresolved.
examples: C: int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); if (p != NULL) { *p = 7; free(p); } — request storage, check success, initialize, use, then release. Include <stdlib.h>.
Rust: { let value = Box::new(7_i32); } — the box owns the value and its storage is cleaned up when the box is dropped.
Go: p := new(int) — obtain a pointer to an int initialized to zero. The spelling does not require heap placement.
counterexamples: Do not transfer a C++ heap-allocation intuition to Go's new: Go chooses placement independently of the syntax.
C++ placement new can construct an object in supplied storage; a new-expression need not obtain a fresh heap block.

assessment.prompt: Compare malloc(sizeof(int)) in C, new int(7) in C++, Box::new(7_i32) in Rust and new(int) in Go. Which value is initialized, who controls storage placement, and what releases it?
rubric: Separate obtaining storage from initializing a value.
Identify the owner or runtime responsible for release without assuming every allocation is a system call.
Explain why Go's new does not imply heap placement and why C++ placement new is a separate case.

C.mechanism: malloc requests a byte count and returns a pointer or NULL on failure. The caller checks success and later releases the block with free. This cell covers positive-size ordinary allocations, not zero-size or over-aligned cases.
C.versionScope: Common positive-size malloc/free behavior documented by Linux libc and Microsoft CRT; checked 2026-09-06.

C++.mechanism: A new-expression creates an object and returns a typed pointer. Ordinary new obtains storage through an allocation function and initializes the object; placement forms can use caller-supplied storage. Do not equate every new-expression with a fresh heap allocation.
C++.versionScope: Core new-expression behavior checked against the working draft and MSVC documentation on 2026-09-06; not an exhaustive allocator or exception treatment.

Rust.mechanism: Box<T> owns heap storage for a value. Dropping the box destroys its value and releases its allocation. Box is useful for recursive structures that need indirection to have a finite size. This cell covers ordinary non-zero-sized boxed values.
Rust.versionScope: Stable standard-library Box and Rust Book documentation inspected 2026-09-06; no unsafe raw-pointer conversion or custom-allocator claim.

Go.mechanism: new(T) returns a pointer to storage initialized to T's zero value. Stack-versus-heap placement is an implementation decision, not a consequence of writing new. The standard toolchain manages heap reclamation with a garbage collector.
Go.versionScope: new(T) semantics and implementation placement checked 2026-09-06. The GC guide explicitly scopes its collector description to the standard toolchain, as of Go 1.19.
